Maths Room / MAKE · LEARN · DISCOVER

Make a repeating pattern.

Find the rule, then keep it going.

Ages 3–815 minAnywhere

A pattern repeats a small unit in the same order. With a handful of large paper shapes, children can copy a rule, predict what comes next and invent a rule of their own. The five Pattern Studio pages below turn each step into a draw-and-save activity.

BEFORE YOU BEGIN

Gather your bits.

A note for grown-ups

An adult can prepare large paper pieces in advance. Avoid beads, buttons or other small loose objects with children who might put them in their mouths.

A little more guidance ↗
ONE STEP AT A TIME

Let's make it happen.

  1. Prepare your pieces

    Tear or cut at least six large shapes in each of two colours. Keep the pieces easy to pick up.

  2. Start a repeating unit

    Place a pink shape, then a yellow shape. Say the order aloud. This pair is your repeating unit.

  3. Keep the rule going

    Repeat the pair three more times. Point to each piece and say the colours. Ask what should come next and why.

  4. Become a pattern detective

    Ask an adult to remove one piece while you look away. Find the gap and explain which piece belongs there.

  5. Invent and swap

    Make a new unit, such as pink-pink-yellow. Repeat it at least three times. Let someone else extend it, then swap roles.

THE LITTLE BIT OF LEARNING

What's happening here?

A repeating pattern has a unit that appears again and again. Recognising the unit is more useful than guessing a single next item: it helps children explain and predict the entire sequence.

Keep the wondering going.

  • What is the smallest part that repeats?
  • Can you clap your pattern instead of showing it?
  • Is pink-pink-yellow the same rule as pink-yellow-pink?

Make it work for you.

Keep it simple

Use two highly contrasting colours and just one shape. Copy a short pattern together, then extend it by one piece.

Take it further

Change two features, such as colour and shape. Write AAB or ABC under each repeating unit and predict the twelfth piece. Then try the Finish My Pattern sheet and check the rules in the answers section.

Not quite going to plan?

If the rule gets lost, separate the repeating units with a little space. Say each unit as a short rhythm before joining the row again.
